Henri & Hélène is a contemporary French bistro inspired by the neighborhood cafés of Paris and the simple pleasure of gathering around the table.

Named after the chef’s two children, the restaurant celebrates elevated French cooking in a warm, playful, setting that’s effortlessly welcoming. Goodside developed a visual identity rooted in vintage French book illustrations, Belle Époque typography, and the soft palette of the French coastline. Hand-drawn engravings inspired by Henri and Hélène weave through the brand, creating a charming visual language that extends across menus, matchbooks, coasters, signage, and printed ephemera. The result is a neighborhood bistro that feels both nostalgic and refreshingly contemporary.

JKR Unveils KFC Bucketverse Branding

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.
  • The move is simple and hard to argue with.
  • Recent findings suggest that two custom typefaces carry the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.

The move is simple and hard to argue with. Instead of inventing a upcoming symbol, JKR took the one object every KFC customer already knows and made it the system. The bucket is now a frame: it holds food photography, illustration and campaign lines, and it scales from a cup to a building. The logo itself turns three dimensional, the Colonel gets a warmer expression and a collar under his bow tie, and the red, white and black palette stays exactly where it was. Nothing about the brand gets thrown out. Everything gets pointed at the bucket.

Recent findings suggest that two custom typefaces carry the voice. Kentucky Fried Serif and Kentucky Fried Sans were drawn with StudioDRAMA, and the serif does the heavy lifting: it spells KFC at poster scale on the bucket, the bag and the building, with thick strokes and tight spacing that read from across a street. The stripes, once a background pattern, are reworked into a type-based asset that carries its own messages, and the boxes repeat lines like BIG KFC FLAVOR DIALED UP TO 11 and NOTHING HITS LIKE KFC ORIGINAL CHICKEN in stacked red caps. Tobias Hall drew the Finger Lickin' Good lettering, which now works as a mark in its own right, set in script against the block serif.

Sources indicate that the system holds together because the same decisions repeat at every size. The kraft bag carries the serif wordmark at full height. The restaurant facade draws the bucket outline across the whole frontage in white line on red, with the Colonel sitting above the door. Inside, curved screens run giant red letterforms behind the counter, and the KWENCH drinks range gets its own vertical sign. A global roster of illustrators adds the colour: Bernardo Henning's loose, bright drawing fills the back of a black T-shirt, and a silver bucket pendant turns the packaging into jewellery. The photography follows the same rule, shot from inside the bucket looking up, so the food and the people sit inside the frame the brand built.

Content warning: this episode has some discussion of sexual and homophobic violence.

Zanele Muholi, Zanele Muholi, Tembisa, Johannesburg, 2014, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

Industry observers note that zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

In a recent development, the people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have stated. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

In a recent development, zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

Zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

According to recent reports, they discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?

This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.

Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with newly introduced guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. You can also explore the related exhibition in La Petite Galerie, called Everyday Clothing, which allows young visitors and families to explore the creative process through works from the MEP’s collections.

The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface

📅 2026-09-09 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, that contract is officially changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, that contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a newly introduced generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our users to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.

This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.

The ultimate goal of modern web design is no longer to build prettier buttons or flashy animations; it is to eliminate the interface entirely.

Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.

It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.

To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.

Consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:.

This is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.

It has been revealed that intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?

When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.

Industry observers note that this shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.

In a recent development, traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.

Perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.

For years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.

Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.

Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent users or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.

Industry observers note that when you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:.

Recent findings suggest that an invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.

Recent findings suggest that in traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store shows the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.

As highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a latest UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.

Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering customers with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).

Intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.

While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.

When a website makes decisions for you, it can quickly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.

Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).

In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the problem — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.

Sources indicate that with an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so customers can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.

As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.

Rather than designing static buttons and rigid forms, we need to learn to map and present dynamic, generative UI components that adapt on the fly to user intent.

By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.

According to recent reports, for decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.

Industry observers note that the philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,.

In a recent development, we are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.

According to recent reports, A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

It has been revealed that the critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, New York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

In a recent development, you need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

Recent findings suggest that the term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

Sources indicate that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

It has been revealed that nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, Upcoming Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

Sources indicate that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:.

A will alone is likely sufficient if:.

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:.

Add irrevocable trust structures if:.

According to recent reports, remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that the most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate proposal.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate initiative should include a pour-over will.

Recent findings suggest that A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific problems or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

In a recent development, A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

Industry observers note that A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Sources indicate that without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

According to recent reports, the living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate strategy is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

#160514. Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK. After graduating from the University of London with a Masters Degree … More about Alex ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

According to recent reports, and proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS manufacturer, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

It has been revealed that companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

Industry observers note that most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch users struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the firm’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of upcoming users’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

Recent findings suggest that one warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

Recent findings suggest that direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in new syncs and shared dashboards.

The line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.

According to recent reports, add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own.

According to recent reports, most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the fresh pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles.

After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing: run the old experience against the new one on an even traffic split until the sample means something.

According to recent reports, onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of upcoming trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established.

Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation.

A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example.

The team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with.

Industry observers note that leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone.

So what did Meridian actually earn? The tech giant sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in latest ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000.

Sources indicate that set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force.

Three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts new ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was.

What persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides.

Budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process, but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.”.

Recent findings suggest that A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI. Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard. Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in newly introduced ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost.

Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid.

Scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows.

It has been revealed that meridian could say that NPS among trial users on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one.

Brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare, and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers.

Recent findings suggest that whatever you collect, systematize the collecting. Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present.

UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to company-wide objectives, so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation.

Industry observers note that nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for: the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment.

This topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX.

A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact, which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit.

When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight consumers, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

  • Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sources indicate that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”.

According to recent reports, I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a new feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

Kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

The bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

Note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

Sources indicate that the viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

It has been revealed that I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”.

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:.

This changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

See the Pen [Viewport vs Container [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73d-6f39-709f-8dae-037f6b588852) by Vayo.

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

Media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

Container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

Industry observers note that an element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

In case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

Industry observers note that I’m not hating on media queries. It’s that in this era of responsiveness and component re-use, layout logic is closer to the container than the viewport. When we think in terms of containers and components, we’re effectively relying on the content to determine layout, not the viewport.

Recent findings suggest that responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

It has been revealed that this works until that same component is moved into a different context, like a sidebar, where the viewport is completely irrelevant. Now, because we tied the responsiveness to the wrong reference point, the scaled typography can get too significant or too small.

Container queries come with their very own units — cqi, cqw, cqb, among others — and we can take responsive components further by coupling those units with the CSS clamp() function, using it for fluid typography that scales with the component rather than the viewport:.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

With this in place, the entire code is self-contained to that element’s specific container.

In a recent development, interestingly, container queries can, in a way, detect the state of a component’s internal layout. It’s not bulletproof, but it is also something media queries simply cannot do because they only observe the external browser window and are structurally blind to internal layout events like when, for example, flex items wrap onto a fresh line. Let’s poke at that.

Flexbox is superb at wrapping content (flex-wrap: wrap), allowing flex items to automatically wrap to new lines when the flex container runs out of space to fit them in a single row. But CSS by itself can’t tell when that wrap happens. There isn’t something like a :wrapped pseudo-class or a media query like @media (flex-wrapped: true) that would get us there.

Media queries only observe the browser window, as they can’t see internal changes. That is pretty much what flex wrapping is: a width state change on the item itself.

In a recent development, for example, if you have a horizontal menu that is lined up with flexbox and you want the items to restyle themselves only when wrapped, you’d be in JavaScript territory, using ResizeObserver to get that information. However, when we nest container queries inside flex items, we can come up with a workaround to get what we need without JavaScript, thanks to this technique I learned from Kevin Powell. The core idea is to allow a flex item to flex-grow: 1 when we query the container’s inline size.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

Industry observers note that this works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles.

See the Pen [Flex Wrap Detection Using Container Queries [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a752-150a-754e-a77a-07fe1b046658) by Vayo.

Container queries, like all things, come with some side effects or caveats you will want to watch for before reaching for them.

In a recent development, container queries need something similar to a parent-child relationship to function as expected. Let’s say we have this markup:.

We can’t actually query the .card component to adjust the .card-content, like this:.

This doesn’t work because a container cannot query itself. In that last example, we’re querying a card container and then attempting to adjust that container’s display based on its size. It’s an infinite loop.

Instead, we need an additional wrapper that makes the .card a descendant of the container:.

From there, we can query the .cards container and adjust the .card layout accordingly:.

Industry observers note that in media queries, this doesn’t matter as @media does not care which element you style inside the block; its only concern is the viewport, which is always available. So you can just slap a condition on any element and call it a day.

This happens when querying the container’s size (i.e., its block, or vertical, size) instead of its inline-size:.

Why? Because the browser calculates the container’s dimensions without looking at its children. If we don’t give the .hero-banner an explicit height (or min-height or aspect-ratio), the browser sets a height of 0px.

Sources indicate that for that reason, it’s often better to query a container by its inline-size instead. That is, unless you genuinely need to query the container’s block size.

Media queries aren’t affected by this, as they treat height the same way they treat @media (min-height: ...) does, i.e., ask the viewport and move on.

Another container query limitation: we can’t query against a custom property value:.

This is because custom properties depend on values that cascade down the DOM tree. There’s the possibility that a container query that relies on a custom property can change that same custom property. And it can rapidly get complicated:.

Industry observers note that I don’t think any project should wholesale use @container instead of @media. Media queries still play an important role in responsive layouts. It’s about understanding the separation of concerns.

Sources indicate that I tend to reach for container queries when a component is used in more than one layout context. For example, a .card element could live in a full-width grid or a narrower sidebar. If that’s the case, then we’ll want the component’s content to determine when it adjusts rather than a media query that looks at the outer viewport.

Similarly, I reach for media queries when a component solely exists at the page level. This would be something like a main navigation that always sits at the top of the page. It is directly influenced by the viewport’s size, meaning that the viewport is a reliable reference for when the navigation needs to adjust. Again, it’s all about “macro” layout versus “micro” layouts.

Here’s a diagram for how I reason about which type of query to use:.

At the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “new”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps.

What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

Christie’s acquires British auction house Dreweatts

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christie's announced today it has acquired the British auction house Dreweatts, a move that confirms the enduring appeal of antiques and older collectibles, particularly as profits in other parts of the auction sector remain squeezed.

Sources indicate that both businesses will run as before, Christie’s confirms, with no staffing changes expected as a result of the deal. Dreweatts will retain its name and continue to be run “independently” by its chief executive, Henry House, and chairman Will Richards, according to a Christie's statement. Dreweatts will continue to operate from its salesroom at Donnington Priory in Newbury, Berkshire, with no sales expected to move to London.

Dreweatts, founded in 1759, is best known for country house and estate sales, and its specialist departments covering furniture, Old Masters, ceramics, jewellery, silver, clocks and wine. It holds around 70 sales a year. In 2025, it posted a record total auction turnover of £37.56m (£47.3m with fees)—a 26% increase from its 2024 results. Both Christie’s and Dreweatts are privately owned and do not disclose their profits.

A display ahead of the sale of Patrick and Amabel Lindsay’s collection at Dreweatts.

In a recent development, the acquisition in some ways sees Christie’s backtrack its 2017 decision to close its South Kensington venue, known as Christie's South Kensington or CSK, which specialised in antiques and other traditional collecting categories. This decision was taken as the market for postwar and contemporary art was at its peak, and as the trade chased global expansion and billionaire tastes at the expense of localism and connoisseurship.

Today, auctions of Modern and postwar trophy lots might generate more glamour and headlines than high-volume and lower-value antiques sales, but the overheads for winning these prize consignments devours profit margins. Indeed, many leading industry figures criticised Christie’s decision to close CSK as a shortsighted one that haemorrhaged valuable strongholds of specialist knowledge and alienated potential latest buyers.

In a recent development, christie's president Bonnie Brennan says in a statement that Dreweatts possesses “particular strength in a part of the market that is highly complementary to our own. Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service.”.

This marks the second major acquisition of a smaller auction house by Christie’s in recent years, following the 2024 buyout of the classic car vendors Gooding & Manufacturer.

Christie’s acquires Dreweatts from the advisory firm Gurr Johns, which bought the regional auction house in 2017 for £1.25m, as The Art Newspaper reported at the time. “I believe that Christie’s is the only business with the capacity, experience and shared culture to fulfil the further potential of Dreweatts,”, Gurr Johns chief told the Financial Times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

It has been revealed that the site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

Industry observers note that how would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, right now with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Sources indicate that of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

Recent findings suggest that what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

As Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

Industry observers note that how to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent company of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the latest system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Sources indicate that looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

It’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Industry observers note that features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

Recent findings suggest that A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

The map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

The right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and people. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

It has been revealed that so if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

According to recent reports, we hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

#160506. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2047 w)

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Industry observers note that yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

It has been revealed that sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

The same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses firm-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these latest systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

It has been revealed that I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

One strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more rapidly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

But, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Industry observers note that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a upcoming tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

At a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

Sources indicate that they need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

According to recent reports, I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff demonstrated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a substantial downside… mistakes will be made.

It has been revealed that many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a upcoming tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

According to recent reports, I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

It has been revealed that what they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

Industry observers note that this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Recent findings suggest that look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

Sources indicate that but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Sources indicate that again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

According to recent reports, today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are right now bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

Industry observers note that and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Company data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

The instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it reveals exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

According to recent reports, however, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out upcoming technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.
