Hollywood and Analog Photography Power Kodak’s Fifth Consecutive Quarter of Growth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.
  • After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.
  • The star of the show for the Rochester, New York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

The star of the show for the Rochester, New York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” states Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

“We continue to execute our long-term blueprint and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an important indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

Sources indicate that as Continenza says, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

While Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak states award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

“The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too promptly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film manufacturer routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

According to recent reports, paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few substantial names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

Then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some upcoming, albeit familiar, ones. The firm reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

Between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year, YouTube has changed how it counts views twice — and both occurred within three months of each other, which is shifting the paradigm of expectations for creators and advertisers. It also appears both creepy and desperate on YouTube’s part.

The first adjustment came back in August when YouTube changed when it would count a view, separating the metric into two parts: a standard view as well as an engaged view.

It has been revealed that “A view is now defined as counting from the very first frame — whether that’s a Short appearing in the feed or a long-form video autoplaying on the Home page,” YouTube explains. “An engaged view is defined as clicking to watch or watching past the initial seconds. This has been, and will continue to be, how you qualify to earn (as long as the content is also public).”.

It has been revealed that that engaged view is basically what standard, public views were before the change and remains in place because YouTube wanted to make its view numbers appear larger to the public, but it also didn’t want to have to tie creator payouts to those higher numbers. Basically, YouTube wanted to have its cake and eat it, too.

YouTube claims it changed the way it counts public views because it wanted to standardize metrics across formats and therefore measure audience reach more accurately. In short, because Meta and TikTok count views instantly on short-form content, YouTube felt like its view numbers on long-form content weren’t keeping up with the times.

In a recent development, this does, at least from YouTube’s perspective, make sense. Short-form has become a huge part of how people consume content now, for better or for worse. While YouTube Shorts are not nearly as popular as Instagram Reels or TikTok, YouTube does have them, and separating how it counted views there to be in line with the competition without adjusting them on long-form felt disjointed.

It’s the second view change YouTube made in 2026 that feels, as I said at the top, particularly creepy and desperate. Starting earlier this month, YouTube started estimating how many people are in the room with a viewer when they play a video on a television and counting those estimations toward the public view count.

According to recent reports, “TVs are usually shared devices where friends, families, and communities come together to watch their favorite content. Until now, one TV playback has only counted as a single public view, even if several people watched together on the same living room screen. By updating public view counts to include co-views, we’re solving this measurement gap, better aligning with long-standing TV industry standards, and telling a more accurate story of how viewers watch your content,” YouTube claims.

When first hearing how YouTube is approaching this, it sounds like YouTube is finding some way to actually see into living rooms. YouTube says this isn’t the case and it doesn’t actually know how many people are sitting in front of the television. Instead, it uses a video’s genre, audience demographics, and the time of day to guess. If YouTube thinks the video attracts a group and it is being watched in the evening, it will use that data to estimate more than one viewer.

“Co-view rate works as a ratio to show how estimated co-views contribute to your overall public views. For example, a Co-view rate of 1.10 means that for every 1,100 views of a video on TV, 1,000 are primary views from the device playback and 100 come from co-viewing,” YouTube explains.

Sources indicate that okay, sure, but why? It just seems like YouTube is obsessed with increasing its view counts to pump up how the platform is perceived while simultaneously not giving creators anything upcoming. None of these changes actually affect revenue for YouTubers.

In a recent development, “This change only updates public view counts. Your actual creator earnings, ad revenue splits, and YouTube Partner Program (YPP) requirements remain unchanged,” YouTube stipulates regarding co-views.

That’s the part that really stands out. Sure, not giving more revenue based on the new calculation of a standard view from August makes sense. That’s not an additional person or viewer more than before; it’s just a new way of deciding at what point the view starts. Fine.

Recent findings suggest that but if co-views are calculating additional people, there is no reason why those views shouldn’t count toward earned revenue. Those are, factually, additional human eyes seeing those videos.

Instead, YouTube gets to pitch advertisers on massive living-room reach while paying creators strictly on single-device clicks. Until those estimated eyeballs translate into actual ad revenue, co-views feel less like a win for creators and more like creative accounting designed to make YouTube look bigger than it is.

I guess when investors are demanding constant growth and the number of humans whose eyes can actually watch content does eventually reach a finite point, the only option is to just make up more eyes.

Breaking: Lisa Marei Schmidt appointed to lead Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lisa Marei Schmidt has been appointed as the fresh director of two major museums in Bern: Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee.
  • Schmidt has directed the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, home to the world’s largest collection of works by artists from the German Expressionist group Die Brücke, since 2017.
  • Born in 1978, Schmidt studied art history in Marburg, Amsterdam and Berlin, and curating contemporary art at the Royal College of Art in London.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lisa Marei Schmidt has been appointed as the fresh director of two major museums in Bern: Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee. The board of trustees of the foundation that oversees both institutions selected Schmidt from 97 applicants following an international search, according to a release. She will lead on artistic direction and also chair the museums' management board.

Schmidt has directed the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, home to the world’s largest collection of works by artists from the German Expressionist group Die Brücke, since 2017. During that time she has co-curated exhibitions exploring complex and sometimes dark aspects of the history of German Expressionism, such as Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019) and Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22). Under her direction, the museum has also strengthened its work in provenance research, restoration, art education and digitisation. The German Association of Art Critics (AICA) named the Brücke-Museum as its museum of the year for 2023.

Born in 1978, Schmidt studied art history in Marburg, Amsterdam and Berlin, and curating contemporary art at the Royal College of Art in London. Before joining the Brücke-Museum, she worked as a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and served as a curator at Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. In 2020, she curated Bonzo's Dream by Swiss artist Vivian Suter, which received AICA's Special Exhibition award.

Sources indicate that “To me, museums are places where art and people meet,” Schmidt said in a statement. "They provide space for encounters, newly introduced perspectives and dialogue across society." She said she looked forward to getting to know the teams in Bern and building on the distinctive qualities of the two museums, which have shared strategic leadership under the umbrella foundation Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee since 2015.

Schmidt will also inherit a pressing challenge at Kunstmuseum Bern. In June, voters in the canton rejected a CHF15.7m (£14.4m) planning credit, or budget allocation, for a project to renovate the museum's historic building and replace its 1983 extension, with 51.8% voting against it. The museum claims its ageing buildings still urgently need repairs.

Schmidt succeeds Nina Zimmer, who led the institutions for a decade and will become director-general of Vienna's Belvedere in January 2027. The foundation’s commercial director Thomas Soraperra will serve as interim director until Schmidt arrives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The category winners for the Illume Awards have been revealed, an extreme sports photography competition built on the legacy of Red Bull Illume.
  • For 20 years, Red Bull turned the Illume Awards into the most recognizable competition for adventure and action sports photography.
  • This year, it is just the Illume Awards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The category winners for the Illume Awards have been revealed, an extreme sports photography competition built on the legacy of Red Bull Illume.

For 20 years, Red Bull turned the Illume Awards into the most recognizable competition for adventure and action sports photography.

This year, it is just the Illume Awards. But the breathtaking images keep coming; check out this year’s category winners below.

French photographer Louis Garnier has won the Snow Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photo of skier Kevin Rolland captured in front of a fire fountain in Tignes, France.

Recent findings suggest that “The energy around the whole project was incredible. We only had three attempts with the flames, and it is still my favorite photo I’ve ever made with Kevin”, he recounts about the day the winning photo was taken.

Austrian photographer Tom Klocker takes the title in the Climb Category with his photograph of climber Mario Andexlinger in Iceland, selected as the winning image from 20 Climb Category Finalists.

According to recent reports, “This shot was very challenging, and you had to have extremely good ice climbing experience. The mystical atmosphere that day went perfectly with the colors,” states Klocker about the making of the photograph.

French photographer Tim Rochas has won the Aerial Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of paraglider Pierre Bottero flying alongside Factory Butte in Utah, United States.

Captured from another glider in flight, the image places the pilot against the vast, rugged desert landscape, creating a striking contrast between the scale of nature and the small human presence in the air.

It has been revealed that the story behind the winning photograph began with a flight from the top of Factory Butte. As the pilots took to the air above the extraordinary desert landscape, Rochas saw an opportunity to capture Bottero alongside the immense rock formation.

“For me, this image is about the contrast between the fragility of a human in flight and the raw power of nature,” he indicates.

Portuguese photographer Beatriz Ryder is the winner of the Surf Category of The Illume Awards 2026. Her photograph of surfer Shaley Mercado in the Solomon Islands was selected as the winning image from 20 Surf Category Finalists.

Recent findings suggest that “We were in one of the most remote parts of the world, the Solomon Islands. Right in front of where we were staying was this little wave – shallow, fast, and with short, fun runners,” claims Ryder about the location behind her winning photograph.

Spanish photographer Ágata Dominguez has won the Trail Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with her captivating photo of late athlete Ida Amelie Robsahm captured in Sancti Spiritu, Spain, during the Zegama-Aizkorri Race 2026, a legendary trail running race.

According to recent reports, “What I love most about photography is being there for the moments that are difficult to explain afterwards, capturing that look, that movement, and that energy in a split second: the tension, the concentration, and the feeling of being completely immersed in what’s happening. I’m not just interested in getting the perfect shot; I would like my images to make you feel something and, ideally, make you feel like you were there,” she explains her approach to photography.

German photographer Robert Christ takes the title in the Skate Category with his photograph of skater André Gerlich in Germany, selected as the winning image from 20 Skate Category Finalists.

Robert Christ’s photo captures André Gerlich performing a backside air trick on a sculpture by Andreas Kiessling in southern Germany.

“André and I found out about a sculpture bike path and immediately made prepares to go there. André chose to skate this rough piece of concrete, did a stylish backside air, and we got a photo we were both really stoked about,” Christ states.

American photographer Lear Miller has won the Bike Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of Hannah Bergemann, captured as part of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon project in Pacific City, Oregon, United States.

Sources indicate that getting the photo was not easy, as Miller explains, “We shot the bike segment of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon over four nights, from about 10 pm to 4 am, in some pretty brutal rain. The riders were riding in the dark while we constantly battled water on the lenses and gear.”.

Chilean photographer Gonzalo Robert Parraguez has been named the winner of the Adventure Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of kayaker Aniol Serrasolses in Svalbard, Norway.

The photo captures Aniol Serrasolses descending a waterfall in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

“We always talk about the photo, but we rarely talk about the athletes, and I dedicate this 100% to Aniol; he was the one who pushed for this whole project to happen, so that we could be taking these incredible photos in the middle of the Arctic”, notes Parraguez.

For more on the contest, head to the Illume Awards website.

Missouri has opened an investigation into a photography business after allegedly leaving numerous customers without the pictures they paid for or a refund.

According to a report by First Alert 4, Leave It to Beaver Photography — a professional family, newborn and wedding photography business based in Wentzville, Missouri — unveiled it had closed this week after 13 years in business.

Sources indicate that however, numerous customers have contacted First Alert 4 with complaints about the company. Some allege they paid for photography services covering events such as weddings, births and anniversaries, but never received their photographs or a refund.

It has been revealed that kristen Moran alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to take family photographs during a Memorial Day weekend camping trip. She also contracted the organization for a maternity shoot in July.

Moran noted the photographs were supposed to be delivered within 20 days, but they did not arrive as promised.

Sources indicate that “It came to months and months of her saying oh I have them, don’t worry about it. Just kind of getting the runaround,” Moran tells the news outlet.

Moran stated the photographs eventually arrived in late October, but by then she had already given birth and no longer needed the maternity images.

Recent findings suggest that “Late October she did send me the photos. She sent me like 300 of them. I was like okay, great. They’re not really relevant anymore, I already had my baby,” Moran notes.

In another case, Monica Dannegger alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to photograph her wedding on December 12, 2026. Dannegger indicates she paid the business $1,500, representing half the cost of photographing her wedding and an engagement party. However, she alleges the photographer did not attend the engagement party and that she has received no communication about the wedding. Dannegger also says she has been unable to obtain a refund.

“It’s unfortunate that her end of the bargain isn’t being upheld,” Dannegger tells First Alert 4. “I would have been left high and dry.”.

The Missouri attorney general has reportedly opened an investigation into the photography business, which operates in St. Charles County. The office is encouraging customers who believe they have been affected to file a complaint through its website. Wentzville police have also advised customers who paid for services they did not receive to file a police report. Officers say they will investigate.

First Alert 4 notes it had contacted Leave It to Beaver Photography for comment but had been unable to reach the photographer.

The news comes a wedding photographer was ordered to pay $1.7 million by the North Carolina Attorney General after leaving hundreds of customers without the services they paid for.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive fresh exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.
  • According to recent reports, simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m.
  • The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive fresh exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.

According to recent reports, simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m. At the heart of the show is the relationship between the three painters, principally the influence of Titian on the two younger, Flemish painters.

The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.

While works by Titian, Rubens and Van Dyck are “very, very difficult to find”, Milo Dickinson notes, there are still some at large thanks to all three being extremely prolific. “Titian was this great role model to Rubens and then Van Dyck, both as a man who was a successful artist throughout his life, courted by major patrons, but also as a painter: the colours he used, the compositions he devised,” Dickinson says. Rubens, for instance, “spent several months just copying paintings by Titian in Madrid, which had been bought by Phillip II of Spain.” As for Van Dyck, the sketchbook he took around Italy when he was a young man is full of annotated studies of Titians.

The exhibition includes several recent rediscoveries, most made after cleaning, with the catalogue outlining the arguments in favour of the attributions made by various experts.

Peter Paul Rubens, Study of the young Anthony van Dyck (around 1616-7).

Courtesy: Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

Sources indicate that among them is what is thought to be a late self-portrait by Titian, variously dated by scholars to between 1546-47 to 1560. The attribution has been long debated by scholars, Milo Dickinson states. Everett Fahy, the American art historian and former director of the Frick who died in 2018, first proposed the attribution to Titian in 2009 when the painting emerged—filthy—from a French private collection. The oil on canvas, small at 44cm by 33cm, was sold for $69,850 at Sotheby's Latest York in 2024, catalogued as “attributed to Titian”. It has subsequently been cleaned, X-rayed and further studied. Now, Dickinson says, “various scholars—Peter Humfrey, Nicholas Penny and Ian Kennedy—have written on it and debated the dating of it because [if the attribution is correct] it would make it one of only three accepted self-portraits by Titian”, alongside those in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin and that in the Prado, Madrid. The painting, which has been in a UK private collection since 2024, is now priced at £1.5m.

According to recent reports, another find is a Rubens head study which is now thought to depict a young Anthony van Dyck, based on dating, the sitter’s distinctive features and comparison with van Dyck’s self-portraits. The oil on panel, which measures 43cm by 35cm, was bought by the current owner at Sotheby’s Paris last November as part of the sale of the collection of the British property billionaire Manny Davidson. Catalogued as a Head Study of a Boy by Rubens, it sold for €744,000. With fitting circularity, Davidson had bought the painting as “attributed to Rubens” in 2007 from Simon Dickinson in 2007, who had spent several years trying to prove it was by Rubens.

In a recent development, the study had been thought to date to around 1614, when Van Dyck would have been only 14 or 15 years old, younger than the boy depicted here with his wispy stubble. But the Louvre, which holds the other half of this double head study, has recently argued that its sketch probably dates to 1616-17. “That got us thinking,” Dickinson states. “Once you've seen it cleaned, you realise the hair colour, the distinct shape of the face, the lips, the shape of the nose, they're totally concurrent with what Van Dyck looked like in his self-portraits.” He adds that Jonckheere and Van der Stighelen support the identity of the sitter as being van Dyck, alongside other scholars. The head study is for sale, price undisclosed.

Brunaille equestrian study by van Dyck (around 1629-32).

According to recent reports, courtesy Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

Yet another post-clean rediscovery is a study by van Dyck for the equestrian portrait of Albert de Ligne, Prince of Arenberg and Barbançon (around 1629-32) which hangs in Holkham Hall, Norfolk. It is one of several similar brunaille studies, one of which is the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Another of these sketches, presumed to be the original, had been in the De Craecker collection in the 19th century but had since gone missing. “Then this one appeared in an American private collection and it was pretty clear, upon seeing it cleaned, that this was the original and the other versions were copies done in Van Dyck's studio by assistants.” Dickinson notes.

In a recent development, he adds that “the sheer quality, the way that he uses highlights, the abbreviated forms” in this version are superior when compared to the others. The pentimenti (revisions) in this, typical of Van Dyck, have also become clearly visible over time, Dickinson says, particularly the adjusted position of the horses head and front legs. The American collector, who bought it in 2014, is now selling the sketch through Dickinson, with an asking price in the region of £500,000.

At the top end of the price range is a friendship portrait by Titian, offered at £3m. Portrait of a young man with a gloved hand (around 1550) is thought to have been the portrait by Titian that is mentioned in van Dyck’s posthumous inventory. It was last publicly exhibited in 1939-40.

The exhibition will travel to Latest York for the Master Drawings New York art fair in (29 January–6 February 2027).

Leica has partnered with British camera bag manufacturer Billingham to introduce two new camera bags designed specifically for its mirrorless cameras.

The new bags come in two sizes: a compact version designed for the Leica M and Q cameras, and a larger model intended for the Leica SL system, such as this year’s Leica SL3-P. Both feature interiors tailored to their respective camera systems, with space for a camera with an attached lens and an additional lens.

According to recent reports, each bag also includes dedicated pockets for SD and CFexpress cards, an internal mesh pocket for accessories, and customizable dividers to keep equipment organized and accessible. An exterior strap allows the bags to be attached to a luggage trolley, making them easier to transport when traveling.

Both models are manufactured in the U.K. using Billingham’s FibreNyte, a proprietary waterproof synthetic material, combined with leather detailing. The bags are available in three color combinations: black, sage/black, and khaki/chocolate.

The Billingham for Leica M/Q bag and Billingham for Leica SL bag will be available from today (November 26, 2026) at selected Leica stores worldwide and through the Leica online store.

The M/Q model has a recommended retail price of £300 ($395) / €350, while the larger SL version costs £380 ($500) / €450.

#160421. How a Photographer Got a Credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram Account

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

How a Photographer Got a Credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram Account

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A photographer has revealed how he managed to get a credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram account after the star initially reposted his video without any attribution.
  • Los Angeles-based David Christopher Lee has been a celebrity portrait photographer for 27 years, capturing stars like Lady Gaga, the Kardashians, and Britney Spears.
  • Recent findings suggest that on November 19, Lee attended the premiere of Jennifer Lopez’s The JLo Show at Paramount Studios in Hollywood as a guest of his friend Maximillian Acevedo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A photographer has revealed how he managed to get a credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram account after the star initially reposted his video without any attribution.

Los Angeles-based David Christopher Lee has been a celebrity portrait photographer for 27 years, capturing stars like Lady Gaga, the Kardashians, and Britney Spears.

A post shared by Jennifer Lopez (@jlo).

Recent findings suggest that on November 19, Lee attended the premiere of Jennifer Lopez’s The JLo Show at Paramount Studios in Hollywood as a guest of his friend Maximillian Acevedo. Lee indicates he had no intentions of taking any photographs or videos at the event.

However, when Lopez came out on the red carpet, photographers rushed out to take pictures, and Lee couldn’t resist shooting some images of the star herself. Lee moved behind the crowd of photographers to find a different angle of Lopez. He noticed Lopez’s yellow diamond necklace and zoomed in to capture a 13-second video on his iPhone at 5x zoom.

The lighting was particularly good, illuminating Lopez’s jawline and earring, and Lee states he immediately knew he had captured the shot he wanted.

“As all the photographers started calling her name. I bolted for the red carpet and stood in the back looking for the perfect angle and whipped out my iPhone, shooting it on 5x,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “My eyes immediately went to her necklace so I framed it like a jewelry shot and the rest is history. I posted the video immediately on Instagram and it immediately went viral.”.

Lee posted the video to his Instagram account (@davidsguide) at 6:25 PM that day. A few hours later, Lopez’s own Instagram account reposted Lee’s clip to her 239 million followers without crediting or tagging him.

Recent findings suggest that lee initially did not realize Lopez had reposted his video because the sound was different. But he eventually recognized his camera movement.

Industry observers note that “At first I didn’t know it was my video because the sound was different,” Lee says. “Then I noticed the same movement of my camera and compared them side by side. I was in shock that she had posted it to her 239 million followers, the only video from that night.”.

Lee states he felt both pleased that his video had gone viral and upset that it was shared without credit, leaving viewers unaware he had filmed it.

In a recent development, “Out of the 100 photographers and videographers there, she had posted my video. I was sad and happy at the same time,” Lee explains. “The video was getting millions of views, and nobody knew I shot it. I felt violated because I’m entertainment, the least someone can do is credit you for using your content.”.

Rather than let the video circulate without credit, Lee took matters into his own hands, contacting several members of Lopez’s team before reaching her social media manager, who agreed to credit his work.

“I reached out to everyone I could find on her team and finally got in touch with her social media manager after five million views,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “I emailed him asking him to credit, and within ten minutes, he replied sorry and gave credit in the video. I felt so accomplished at that point.”.

As of writing, Lopez’s repost, which now includes Lee’s Instagram tag @davidcleephotography, has over 350,000 likes and over 9,600 comments. Lee states that reposting content without attribution can give it a wide audience while leaving the original photographer unrecognized. He believes photographers frequently have their work shared without credit because content spreads so promptly online that people sometimes forget to acknowledge its creator.

“It happens all the time,” Lee notes. “Content moves and travels so fast these days that a lot of times people forget to tag and credit. It is unfortunate, but it’s the world we live in.”.

Lee encourages photographers to learn from his experience and take precautions when sharing their work on social media. He advises them to watermark their images and videos before posting, as they never know how widely the content might be shared.

“The lesson is you never know what can happen with your content and the best thing to do is watermark your pics or videos before posting,” Lee notes.

In a recent development, he adds: “Keep doing what you do and do stop believing in yourself. The possibilities are endless.”.

More of David Christopher’s work can be found on his website and blog David’s Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the world of movie posters, floating-head designs are among the most hated trends, and arguably no studio is more guilty of this creative sin than Marvel. Now, it seems it hasn't learned from its past, only doubling down on this disliked design with its upcoming Doomsday poster.

Industry observers note that take a look at the best movie posters of all time, and you're unlikely to see a floating head. They're formulaic and overplayed, so it's no surprise that when Marvel dropped the Doomsday poster, fans understandably tore it to shreds.

Industry observers note that doomsday is already one of Marvel's most hyped releases since the End Game days, so you'd hope it'd bring a poster to match the energy. Instead, we've been blessed with a strange, overcrowded floating head design, muddied by an incessant shade of green.

Industry observers note that "Bruh, this looks like the direct-to-video, bottom of the barrel s**t you saw at Walmart in 2004 and what you see on page 8 of your Prime Video search results," one scathing critic wrote. Investigation Reveals Who Betrayed Photographer Secretly Documenting Nazi-Occupied France

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.
  • In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.
  • Industry observers note that raoul Minot.1940-42.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.

In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.

Industry observers note that raoul Minot.1940-42. Paris occupé WW2 pic.twitter.com/SBnUj87HWA.

— Paris Paname (@ParisAMDParis) August 24, 2024.

It has been revealed that le Monde journalist Philippe Broussard began a four-year investigation to identify the photographer, who had taken at least 700 pictures of Paris during the first two years of the Occupation. At the time, unauthorized photography was banned by the Nazis, and taking such pictures could carry the death penalty. In 2024, Broussard identified the photographer as Raoul Minot.

Minot used a “little Kodak Brownie 6/9 camera” and developed the prints in the photographic laboratory of the department store where he worked. He then sold hundreds of his images to the French Resistance, a collection of groups that fought against the Nazi occupation during World War II.

However, Minot’s photographic mission came to an end in November 1942, just two years after it began, when an unidentified informer reported his activities to the Nazis.

Recent findings suggest that minot was imprisoned and deported to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria on April 20, 1943, where he was forced to perform labor. He was later transferred to Flossenbürg concentration camp in Bavaria and liberated by U.S. forces on April 23, 1945. He tragically died five days later in a hospital in Cham, Bavaria.

According to recent reports, following his discovery of Minot in 2024, Broussard set out to uncover who had turned in the photographer to the Nazis for a report in Le Monde. A breakthrough came in April 2026, when a reader contacted Le Monde with a document that could help solve the mystery. Jean-Pierre Gross, a local history enthusiast from Courbevoie, France, had discovered a 1944 report accusing two of Minot’s neighbors, Marie Breux and Georges Robinson, of collaborating with the Germans and helping secure the arrests of people suspected of opposing the Occupation.

The report specifically named Minot, stating that the couple were suspected of having “denounced or, at the very least, incriminated” him. It also claimed they had boasted about getting 18 people arrested.

Breux was the building’s concierge, while Robinson, her partner, was a tailor with a history of theft and other criminal convictions. Both were arrested following the Liberation in August 1944, although no record of a conviction against either has been found.

Further investigation revealed that Robinson had briefly worked at the same Printemps department store as Minot, potentially explaining how he knew about the store’s photographic facilities.

Broussard later uncovered an anonymous letter sent in December 1942 that accused Minot and his wife of photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage. The letter prompted a police investigation that led to Minot’s arrest and the seizure of more than 1,000 photographic negatives.

“Sir, could you ask the Minot household, both of whom work at the Printemps — the wife as a cashier, the husband as a warehouse manager — whether their jobs qualify them to take photographs of propaganda posters and air raid damage to our poor country?” the letter reads. “We don’t think it would be very useful to inform you about the troubled times France is going through, thanks to many workers in troubled waters.

Industry observers note that according to Le Monde, a handwriting expert subsequently ruled out Robinson as the author of the anonymous letter that triggered the investigation into Minot, but could not exclude Breux. Broussard believes the couple may have worked together to report Minot after discovering that he was photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage around Courbevoie.

Although there is still no conclusive evidence to establish who sent the letter, Broussard’s investigation has brought researchers closer than ever to identifying the people who may have brought Minot’s secret photographic mission to an end.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Arkivism Is a Searchable Archive of More Than Four Million Free Public Domain Images

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new website called Arkivism aims to make searching for historical imagery considerably easier by bringing more than four million public domain images and videos together in one place.
  • Sources indicate that the free-to-use archive (requires sign-up) includes historical photography from the Library of Congress, NASA imagery, and vintage film reels.
  • Arkivism also has an interface that will feel familiar to Pinterest owners, with an infinite scroll, visual discovery features, and the ability to save images and videos to personal boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new website called Arkivism aims to make searching for historical imagery considerably easier by bringing more than four million public domain images and videos together in one place.

Sources indicate that the free-to-use archive (requires sign-up) includes historical photography from the Library of Congress, NASA imagery, and vintage film reels. Users can search the collection using natural language, describing what they want to find rather than having to know the exact title or filename of an image.

Arkivism also has an interface that will feel familiar to Pinterest owners, with an infinite scroll, visual discovery features, and the ability to save images and videos to personal boards. Users can also extract high-resolution stills from archival video clips.

In a recent development, according to its creator, James, the archive presently contains more than four million full-resolution images and over 27,000 searchable film clips. Each asset also includes a backlink to its original source.

“Arkivism started as a fix for my own problem,” James tells PetaPixel, who explains that he used to edit long-form video documentaries on YouTube for the channel History of the Earth.

In a recent development, “There are millions of incredible public domain assets out there, but they’re scattered across slow, dated archives. Unless you knew the exact filename, finding one specific image could take hours. I wanted one place where I could describe what I needed in plain English and search everything at once.”.

It has been revealed that the project has been developed independently in James’s spare time since July. Despite its size, Arkivism is largely a one-person operation, with AI coding tools helping to make the development process more manageable.

James says the biggest challenge has been building systems capable of collecting material from numerous online sources while ensuring that every asset is properly validated as public domain.

“Above all, every asset has to pass validation checks confirming it’s public domain, because that’s the whole point of the site,” he says.

That emphasis on historical material is also part of the motivation behind the project. With AI-generated imagery becoming increasingly prevalent online, James believes there is particular value in making authentic historical photographs and footage easier to discover.

“I’m not anti-AI, obviously, but there’s real value in looking back, and I think that’s where the site really shines: you can dive endlessly down historical rabbit holes,” he indicates.

Although Arkivism borrows some of its interface design from Pinterest, James sees it as both a searchable archive and a visual discovery platform. Unlike traditional institutional archives, users can browse the collection without necessarily knowing what they’re looking for. Unlike Pinterest, however, the experience is not driven by an algorithm and contains no advertising.

“The site and archive will stay free,” James adds. “But further down the line I plan to build optional paid tools, such as After Effects and Figma plugins that bring the archive straight into editing software.”.

A post shared by ARKIVISM (@_arkivism).

The intended audience extends beyond photographers and filmmakers. Researchers, designers, and anyone looking for historical imagery can use the platform to find and download material, with the reassurance that assets have been checked for public domain status.

Arkivism is available now at Arkivism.com.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has declared.

Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.

In a recent development, she has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.

Industry observers note that she holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.

Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, states in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.

He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.

Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.

Recent findings suggest that since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. In 2025, under his watch, Qatar unveiled it would launch a national pavilion at the Biennale. A temporary structure was used for the most recent architecture and art biennales; the completed pavilion building will be the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale’s two main venues, in 30 years.

In a statement, Al Qasimi says that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.

Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wolff Olins rebuilds the Decathlon brand identity around wonder, L'Orbit and Decathlon Sans, uniting 85 brands into one global sports brand.
  • According to recent reports, the work starts from a blunt observation.
  • According to recent reports, decathlon Sans carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins rebuilds the Decathlon brand identity around wonder, L'Orbit and Decathlon Sans, uniting 85 brands into one global sports brand.

According to recent reports, the work starts from a blunt observation. More than 3 billion people play sport, but the stories around it keep pointing at podiums and perfection. Decathlon, the third biggest sports company in the world with over 2,000 stores, sells to everyone from first timers to pros, and its old identity never noted that out loud. Wolff Olins builds the whole system on wonder instead, the enjoyment, connection and adventure that keep people playing, and one refreshed blue does the talking. It runs from the storefront to the jersey chest to the shoe heel, with the white L'Orbit mark sitting on it, and the system adapts across 70 markets and 85 sports.

According to recent reports, decathlon Sans carries the voice. Grilli Type drew the bespoke grotesque with alternate characters that tilt, stretch and blur, so headlines read as movement before they read as words. MOVE fills a whole frame in leaning white capitals, and Ready to play? scatters across the blue with the question mark drifting off on its own. The wordmark itself is refined rather than redrawn, tightened up and set beside the new symbol. Down at product level the same type turns precise: a Quechua jacket panel pairs the Orbit with Men's Ultralight Hiking Jacket in plain black and white, and spec lines like Ergonomic Cut, for freedom of movement sit next to their icons in a strict two column grid.

In a recent development, the system holds together because every surface plays by the same rules. The Orbit repeats at every scale, set small on a blue training top, printed on a white shoe heel, lit on a blue cube sign on a city street, and running the full width of a store facade. Product cards keep the same discipline online, camp cooking, a ski holiday pack and a trail kit each inside a clean white card with a price and one line of copy, and the website carries the same product lists over full bleed mountain photography. Sustainability gets its own corner of the language too, with green Shop Rental, Second Life and Bring Back marks set against the blue, so repair and reuse read as part of the brand rather than an afterthought.

See more from Wolff Olins on their site.

#160410. Industry News: Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1238 w)

Industry News: Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday!
  • This story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR.
  • PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday! While our Film Fridays tend to spotlight a single emulsion, with this annual celebration we feature the entire selection of black and white film stocks that we have in our inventory. But before we dig in too far, it would be a good moment to explain our inspiration for Film Friday.

This story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR. Blue Moon offers film, development services, printing, and even an ever-rotating line of film cameras and lenses.

PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!

Blue Moon Camera and Machine rolled out Film Friday publicly in 2019, but it had been an ongoing project of ours for several years prior to that. The film that started it all was Ilford XP2. See, we (the collective “we”, that is, as in all of us film photographers) have always had an amazing selection of films to choose from as we decide what to load in our cameras. This selection has evolved over time. Some years it has winnowed down, and other years it has actually expanded. But there have always been just so many films out there to make our work and art with. It is also true, however, that most of us gravitate to certain films. We find the emulsion we like, and we settle into it.

Industry observers note that this is neither a good behavior nor a bad one—perhaps it is both; it is simply what we tend to do. And even when you work in an all-analog camera store, like Blue Moon Camera, you can fall into these patterns. And this is where XP2 comes in. Ilford XP2 was one of those films we never used all that much. To be honest, Kodak Tri-X and Ilford HP5 were our typical go-to film stocks. Yet every now and then we would find cause to shoot with a roll of XP2 instead.

Sources indicate that this might happen two or three times a year. And each of those times we would get the negatives back and think to ourselves, “Wow, XP2 is a gorgeous film. Why don’t we use this stuff more often?” Of course, the answer is because we know what we know, and we like to stick with that. And thus we decided to set about changing this. We made it a personal project to not just shoot a roll of every film we carried, but actually use it repeatedly and get to know it. One film at a time we would go out for several months, working through multiple rolls, taking our time, learning each emulsion’s quirks and characteristics, and then coalescing those experiences into a collection of images and a written review. The goal was to pass along not just the knowledge and experience we had gained, but the inspiration as well.

There is something to be said for working in depth and committing to a single film and knowing it like you know nothing else. But there is also something to be said about breadth and being familiar with all the myriad options open to you in your creative pursuits. And that is the beating heart of our Film Fridays. It is about celebrating the wealth of options open to us. It is about reminding ourselves that there are more films out there than simply Ultramax, Portra, or HP5. And of course, it is about learning and growing as film photographers.

So having remarked all that, we came up with the idea of Black (and White) Film Friday only a few years ago. Yes, it is timed to coincide with Black Friday, and yes, quite admittedly, there is a bit of a commercial gimmick built into that. But there is also more to our B&W Film Friday than the sales angle. Let us explain.

Industry observers note that in a similar way to how many of us gravitate toward a select few film stocks, we have also noticed that, generally speaking, many film photographers lean toward color film photography. This is especially true with newer film photographers. A big reason is we see the world, and our lives, in color, so it is a natural or even reflexive deduction to photograph with color film. Time and again we have had customers at the counter ask for film recommendations, and we, in turn, ask if they are interested in color or B&W film. It is not uncommon for them to respond to that simple question with some surprise that they had not even considered black and white and had never even tried a roll of it. This is the thing with habits; they tend to fit so snugly we can forget they are even there.

But B&W film should not be forgotten or overlooked. In short, there is a classic beauty and a timelessness that can only be captured with B&W film. It also simplifies the world in its way by converting colors that may otherwise be distracting into tones of grey and letting us make images about something other than the reds, oranges, yellows, greens, blues, and violets of the world.

Black and white allows us to focus on light, textures, relationships, shapes, patterns, grit, grain, and so many other elements (or ideas). It isn’t that you cannot do these things with color film—you can—but there is a directness with which B&W lets you approach these things. This is harder to understand via explanation than it is through experience. So we run our B&W Film Friday not just for the photographers who already love their black and white films, but also for those who have never stepped into those waters.

Recent findings suggest that and there is a crazy variety out there to work with. There are more different types of black and white films than there are color films. We did a rough count, and once you eliminate all the different format choices and focus on just the different emulsions, we have at least 45 unique film stocks to try.

Sources indicate that these films are mostly of the black and white negative type, but there are a few reversal films as well and also a couple of black and white instant films to keep in mind. Let’s repeat that number for emphasis: there are at least 45 unique black and white films in our inventory alone. And we don’t even carry every possible B&W film option on the market. That is easily in the 50s and maybe the 60s once you go out into the wider market looking for these films.

Recent findings suggest that so what are you waiting for? That is a lot of film to try, and our guess is most of you have perhaps not even used half of these. So take advantage of this one day where you can pick up more of your favorite B&W film, or you can try something entirely new. We heartily recommend doing both. Visit our online store or come by our shop in St. Johns, Portland, Oregon, and get some film.

Sources indicate that not all kids' tech is evil, and some is pretty darn great. I've found a niche that combines being a parent, my love of design and my years as an early years teacher, and it means I get to test some seriously good products. There are a few I'm firmly recommending, and they'd make great Christmas presents.

Sources indicate that I love the Yoto. I can't shout about this enough. We've been using it for the last seven years, I bought one when my daughter was two, and it's going from strength to strength in functionality and design (read my interview with the team who recently redesigned the hardware). The Yoto does have a screen but is very deliberately only using it to display fun pixel graphics, and the time.

It has been revealed that if you're not familiar, you play stories and music hosted on cards via the Yoto machine – which comes in a full sized and mini version. Cards are available to buy – but you can also make your own cards, which is the major selling point for me. You can record your own content, or you can put MP3 files onto them. There's also an ever-changing library of podcasts and other audio, accessed via an app.

Yoto is currently up to 30% off – and it would make a fabulous Christmas present.

In a recent development, I bang on about the Nex Playground to everyone – my family adores it. It's an active play system that gets players up and moving through its whole body tracking. In my experience, this console counters the usual effect video games or tablets have on children. It encourages discussion, collaboration with its gentle and imaginative games, which include sports like Bowling (my son's favourite), and substantial-name titles like How to Train Your Dragon and Bluey. See our full Nex Playground review here.

If you're thinking about a console for your children this Christmas, I really can't recommend this one enough – and it's also presently got 37% in the UK, and 30% in the US off for Black Friday.

If you've got a younger child interested in 3D printing, this is a great option. As I say in my Funbox review, if your child is at the upper end of the 4-12 age bracket, I'd go for a proper 3D printer. My daughter is on the borderline at 9, but my son (5) would get plenty of life from this printer.

It's a fun design, and is super-simple to use via an app. You can draw designs and let the AI print them, or pick from a marketplace of designs (make sure you use the official UGEE designs for maximum effectiveness). Because it's enclosed, it's safer for kids to use.

It's currently got a small saving of $20 at Amazon.

This is the one I'm yet to try, but I'm so excited by the idea. I join a lot of parents in not wanting my children to have their own phones for a long while yet, but I realised that when I was younger I would be phoning my friends on the landline. We don't have a landline, and I gatekeep my own phone for obvious reasons. So I was searching for a solution – and the Tin Can is perfect.

Sources indicate that pitched as a New-School Landline phone, it connects to the WiFi and only phones/accepts calls from approved numbers (controlled via an app). If another child has a TinCan, they can phone each other for free, and other approved numbers can be called if you pay a monthly subscription.

I've got one on its way to me so I'll be doing a review on it soon, but I wanted to put it on your radar as I think it's such a smart idea. It's out in the US, and preorders are open for before-Christmas delivery in the UK.

Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry.
  • The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • Sources indicate that for many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

Sources indicate that for many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

It has been revealed that whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

It has been revealed that psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

Sources indicate that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

It has been revealed that the relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

It has been revealed that tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It indicates, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.
